newsitem.title: USA: Latest Kevorkian assisted suicide ruled homicide.
newsitem.headline: Latest Kevorkian assisted suicide ruled homicide.

text.p: The death of a Californian woman who eluded police to commit suicide with Dr. Jack Kevorkian's help has been ruled a homicide, the Oakland County Medical Examiner's office said on Monday.

Isabel Correa, 60, from Fresno, died from carbon monoxide poisoning, a spokeswoman for the office said. She did not have information on whether Correa was suffering from a terminal illness. The deputy medical examiner who performed the autopsy was not available.
Correa had said she suffered from a painful spinal cord disorder that confined her to a wheelchair and had left her in constant pain for years.

Correa travelled to Michigan on Friday with her husband and other family members to seek Kevorkian's help in commiting suicide. Acting on a tip, police disrupted the meeting in Correa's motel room and confiscated various chemicals and equipment they said Kevorkian planned to use in her death.

But Correa was steadfast in her desire to end her life, telling reporters on Friday night: "I came to die, and it's so sad that I have to come across the United States to see a man like Kevorkian when there should be one in California."
Correa met again with Kevorkian sometime early on Saturday and took her life with the assistance of the retired pathologist, who then drove her body to a local hospital.

Including Correa, Kevorkian has acknowledged being present at 40 assisted suicides since 1990. But his attorney, Geoffrey Fieger, said there had been other deaths Kevorkian had assisted that were not reported in the media.
An article in Saturday's New York Times said those deaths included a 61-year-old woman of Livonia, Mich., who died August 6, and another person who died in July.
Michigan juries have acquitted Kevorkian three times on assisted suicide charges involving five deaths.
